analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer loan interest rates at 36% for everyone, extending protections now limited to military families.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have capped consumer loan interest at 36%, was introduced with 26 cosponsors and died in the House Financial Services Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, a 2006 law caps interest on loans made to service members and their families at 36% and limits the fees and add-on charges lenders can pile on. This bill would give every American the same protection: no consumer loan could cost more than 36% a year once fees are counted, enforced by federal and state regulators. It would carve out home mortgages, car loans, and federal credit union loans, and it would not override state laws that go further. The bill never received so much as a committee hearing; it died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use payday loans, title loans, installment loans, and high-fee credit cards — disproportionately low-income households, veterans not covered by the existing military cap, and people with thin credit — would keep far more of their money, since loans could not carry rates above 36% once fees are included. Credit unions and lower-cost lenders would gain customers.

how_it_helps.text: It caps the interest rate on consumer credit at 36%, extending to everyone the protections service members already have under the Military Lending Act.
It applies the Military Lending Act's full rulebook to civilian loans — including limits on fees and add-on charges for open-end credit — not just the headline rate cap.
It lets state attorneys general and state regulators sue violators and bars the federal regulator from granting waivers, giving borrowers more enforcement than federal law alone provides.
It keeps stronger state laws in place rather than overriding them with a weaker federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, title lenders, subprime credit card issuers, and other businesses whose model depends on rates far above 36% would lose most of their revenue; some borrowers who rely on these loans might have fewer places to turn for emergency credit, though federal credit union loans and car loans are exempt.

drawbacks.text: The 36% cap would likely push many high-cost lenders out of the market, and some borrowers who rely on payday or installment loans for emergencies could lose access to quick cash if cheaper substitutes do not fill the gap.

The rate cap is a blunt tool: it does nothing to lower the underlying cost of living or to help borrowers qualify for cheaper credit, so the people it protects most are also the people it may leave with nowhere to borrow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial: tens of millions of borrowers with poor or thin credit would stop owing fees and interest that routinely exceed what they borrowed, and the cap already works for the military population it covers. The cost is real: lenders that survive on high-rate credit would shrink or exit, and some borrowers in a pinch might lose the fastest available option. The bill preserves access through credit unions and car loans and lets states add stronger protections, but it offers no replacement channel for the borrowers it removes from the high-cost market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 15, 2021 and referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Had it passed, it would have extended the 36% rate cap and the Military Lending Act's fee rules to all consumer credit, with carve-outs for mortgages, car loans, and federal credit unions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost lenders — payday, installment, and subprime card issuers — are better off, since the bill that would cap their rates at 36% never received a vote.

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the military 36% rate cap to all consumers.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the sole Republican among the initial 26 cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The 26 cosponsors were 25 Democrats and 1 Republican (Glenn Grothman), and the House Financial Services Committee, with a Democratic majority, never moved it to a vote.

industries.note: These lenders rely on rates far above 36%; the cap would eliminate most of their core product, as it already did within the military lending market.
Most mainstream card rates fall under 36%, but the bill would fold fees and add-on products into the capped rate, cutting a profitable revenue stream on subprime and fee-heavy cards.
Federal credit union loans are expressly carved out of the cap, so they could keep serving small-dollar borrowers that high-rate lenders abandon.
Home mortgages and car-purchase loans are exempted, leaving their interest largely untouched.
